data.title: 賴清德總統談年輕人困境
data.transcript_raw: There is a term going around called the  "Three Nothings": no mortgage, no car  loan, and no offspring. Some say the  reason is that the external environment  is just too harsh—so harsh that young  people can't even imagine settling down  or pursuing a career. They might just  choose to "lie flat," not even thinking  about marriage or dating, just getting  by day to day and relaxing. But for the  individual, I don’t think there is  anything wrong with that. Young people  have their own ideas and values, after  all. However, if many young people  think this way, at your level as  President, don’t you think this is a  problem? What would you like to say to  these young people? >> Yes, this is indeed a problem. If the  social atmosphere reaches this point,  it is truly a very >> very significant social issue that  deserves attention, yes. I want to  share an experience with these young  people: while your life certainly  belongs to you, life is not just  divided into stages; it is a journey  spanning decades, perhaps even a  century, from birth to passing. Mm. So,  while you may have one perspective when  you are young, your thoughts might  change if you look at the long term. >> I also hope that everyone can have a  wonderful, fulfilling life that meets  their own needs. >> But as President, my hope is to create  better conditions. >> Mm. Because if I encourage raising  children, then I should build a better  environment for raising them, allowing  young people to feel willing and free  from worry to start families. >> That is why I mentioned the zero-to-18  growth journey earlier; that is just  one part of it. We recently released  our national population strategy,  specifically the family support section . Mm. >> Beyond the zero-to-18 growth journey,  we are focusing on three stages: birth,  raising, and education. We have  proposed childbirth subsidies. And for  affordable childcare, we are also  providing educational subsidies. Then  there is housing. Mm. >> And a friendly workplace. >> In other words, allowing young parents >> to not have to choose between their  family and their work. Of course, what  I’m describing is a concept, but I am  not a scholar.
